messages.subject: Addressing inadequate replication in small forest fragments: repeated-walks procedure
messages.subject_clean: Addressing inadequate replication in small forest fragments: repeated-walks procedure
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

we are designing a study to estimate population densities of spider monkeys living in isolated, small forest fragments in western Ecuador.  However, we are struggling to meet the basic assumption of replication.

Our study fragments range from around 35 ha to 1300 ha. The ridiculous size of some of the smallest fragments precludes any possibility of adequate replication, but we plan to conduct full counts in these patches. However, not even in the larger patches will we be able to achieve adequate replication. Should we increase the number of lines at the expense of reducing line length? From my understanding, we can later increase line length if we carry on repeated surveys of the same line (repeated-walks procedure). Is there a minimum "real" line length we should consider to be able to use "Distance" accurately?  Can we get away with less than 10 lines per fragments and yet have robust results?

Besides, we have realized there is a common trend to prevent transect lines from crossing one another. However, in our field site the shape and the size of the fragments make problematic the establishment of parallel transects. I am wondering if independency of the transects would be reduced if we do place lines crossing one another, but we never census these lines on the same day.

Thank you all for your help.

Best,

Irene Duch-Latorre

PhD Student, Department of Anthropology
Strier Lab – Primate Behavioral Ecology and Conservation
UW-Madison

messages.body_plain:
Irene

Wonderful to hear you are devoting energy to study design for your spider monkey survey.  It is sometimes difficult to place sufficient sampling effort into patches of fragmented habitat.

It is a tenet of distance sampling that many short lines are preferable to few long lines.  There are two reasons for this: assuming transects are placed randomly in the patch, a small number of transects can, by chance, be unrepresentative of the patch as a whole.  Secondly, a small number of transects will make it difficult to estimate variability between transects.  Both of these circumstances compromise the ability to make inference about the patch based upon data collected on the transects.  Recognise that in any type of sampling (distance sampling being a special case), you are attempting to make inference about a phenomenon (in this case monkey density) in places you do not visit.  Your confidence about what might be happening where you do not visit is strengthened by adequate spatial replication.

Your question stating "can we get away with less than 10 lines per fragment and have robust results?" is that you cannot know.

Your comments about crossing transects and repeat visits to transects represent "trading time for space"--repeatedly sampling the same piece of ground does not effectively increase the strength of your inference about what is happening off the transects.  Repeated visits to transects can increase the number of detections, useful in fitting of detection functions, but does not alleviate issues of design-based inference.

Have a read through this paper for more on the subject of survey design in primate studies:
Buckland, S. T., A. J. Plumptre, L. Thomas, and E. Rexstad. 2010. Design and analysis of line transect surveys for primates. International Journal of Primatology 31 (5): 833–47. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10764-010-9431-5.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Distance group,

I am a beginner in distance sampling analysis, so sorry for the naive questions.
I am dealing with mountain herbivores (ibex) data (736 observations) that have been sampled with line transects. The final aim of our projet is to estimate the population abundance to study demographic evolution of the population with time.

My issue relates to the AIC values calculated with the software Distance and the ds function in R. I wanted to compare the two results to be sure I did the right thing in R.

In R, my script looks like :
hr.ip <- ds(d , transect  = "line" , dht.group = F , convert.units = 0.001 , key = "hr" , truncation = list(left = "0%" , right = "5%") , method = "BFGS" , formula = ~ transect)
-> Before, I compared different models and this one above has the lowest AIC (effect of the transect).
The AIC equals 7950.633.

When I do the same thing (MCDS model with transect as covariate, same key function, same truncation) in the software Distance, the AIC equals 7960.2388.

Why is there such a difference ? Consequently, it does not give the same probabilities of detection...

When I do the same thing but with the "halfnormal" function, it gives the same AIC between the software Distance and R (ans so the same probabilities of detection).

Have you ever had this problem ? Is there something related to the hazard rate function ?

If anyone have an idea and can help me, I would be very grateful !

Thank you
Cheers

Marjorie

messages.body_plain:
Marjorie

Welcome to the list.  I'll answer two questions.

First the question you asked:  why different AIC for a model fit using R and a model fit using Distance.  The answer is that the likelihood values are different according to the two different fitting engines.  The optimisation used to estimate the parameters of the hazard rate detection function are not the same, and for complex models, will produce slightly different estimates.  Because the hazard rate model is more complex than the half normal, the differences in the fitting algorithms are likely to be more pronounced with the hazard rate models.  This is a situation with which we are familiar and occurs in other data sets we have analysed.

The question you did not ask:  I've not seen fitting of detection functions with covariates for transects.  Often it is the case that there are insufficient detections per transect to be able to fit such models.  It is also common for there to be a large number of transects such that a large number of parameters are associated with a factor covariate for transect.

messages.body_plain:
Adding to Eric’s comments, there is unlikely to be an advantage to fitting transect as a covariate unless you are estimating density separately for each transect.  Pooling robustness means that you estimate overall density (or abundance) without bias even if the detection function differs by transect – assuming a good survey design, and assuming assumptions hold.  Nevertheless, you may want to fit covariates to the detection function, e.g. observer or habitat, which does then allow the detection function to differ by transect.  Using AIC to investigate different covariate models helps to avoid over-parameterizing.  Given that you have so many detections for each transect, then it may be reasonable to include transect as a factor-type covariate in at least one of your models.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject_clean: Abnormally high abundance and density estimates
messages.body_plain:
I wanted to post to inform everyone the solution to my issues. The first issue stemmed from the set up of the data collection. I learned that it is essential to record transects that are driven, even if no animal is seen. This is represented and taken into account in the analysis by listing the number of visits to each transect, and then multiplying that number by the transect length. I also learned the importance of making sure all units are uniform across the board. One of my issues stemmed from having my transect length in meters and distance was in km. In addition, even once all the data was reformatted, my estimates were still  high with high standard error, probably because the number of detections (25) is very small. The suggested number of detections (Buckland et al. 2001) needed to produce credible density estimates is 60-80 observations. Also, our transects were driven rather than walked at one of our locations, which causes potential bias due to the fact that roads are inherently not random.

messages.body_plain:
If you see the same individual multiple times because you traverse lines multiple times, then the method accounts for that.  Lines (or points) are assumed to be independent, but multiple traverses of the same line are not assumed to be independent.  If you see the same animal multiple times on the same traverse, and you record it as a new detection each time, then you will over-estimate abundance.  If you can identify individuals, then you could incorporate a movement model to exploit the multiple sightings.  I find it difficult to see that there would be much benefit if any of doing so.  To develop an appropriate model, you would need to distinguish the case of the multiple detections being due to chance, from the case that the multiple detections are because an individual animal is responding to you.  Richard Glennie at St Andrews has developed movement models for distance sampling, but not for this purpose – his methods adjust for bias when movement of animals is not slow relative to movement of the observer.

Steve Buckland

Hi all,
Thank you so much for your responses, some useful insights and thoughts there. I do wonder if the SCANS II data were ever analysed to compare ESAS surveys to dedicated cetacean surveys - I'll make some enquires.
Best wishes,
James

On Thursday, November 29, 2018 at 4:57:51 PM UTC, ewan_wa...@yahoo.co.uk wrote:
> Hi James,
>
> These are questions that are frequently asked in the field ( during those long hours spent staring at empty sea) but I'm not aware of anyone having addressed them analytically.
>
> > However, what would happen to the data if more target species were added to these surveys? If seabirds were also recorded, would the detection probability decrease as observers are looking for multiple cue types simultaneously?
>
> During the Scans II survey, at least one ship had both seabird and cetacean observers working simultaneously (but on different platforms). The bird observer recorded cetaceans as well as seabirds. I heard at the time that these data were going to be analysed to see if cetacean abundance estimates made using data collected using the ESAS survey method were similar to those made using dedicated cetacean surveys. I'm not sure if this analysis ever happened - someone from SMRU would know. If not, the data should be there to analyse...
>
> >
> > Similarly, I was wondering if recorded numbers of one taxa and accuracy may decline due to surveyors counting a flock of birds when dolphins were passing by, leaving less time to count them and collect accurate bearings etc? I suppose this would depend upon the density of animals in the area, but I'm imagining a feeding flock scenario that is also attended by dolphins or whales.
>
> This can definitely be an issue during ESAS-style surveys. As James suggests, a clear protocol goes some way to standardising data collection is such scenarios. Experienced surveyors tend to be be better at keeping a cool head when confronted with big muti-species feeding aggregations. In terms of analysis, one could consider association with other species as a covariate. In fact, I've just been looking at this and some small seabirds definitely become more detectable when they're associated with other seabirds or cetaceans.
>
> >
> > On a smaller-scale, is there any merit collecting data on a single target species as opposed to a family or order? Say for example if a survey was collecting data on fin whales, is there any evidence that the data would be better than if observers collected data on all cetaceans? I wonder if a bit of variety and more frequent sightings (within reason) may keep observers awake!
>
> On most ship-based surveys, multi-species groups of cetaceans occur so infrequently that there's little chance of missing one species because observers are focused on another. That said, a potential issue with primary platform observers is that they can spend so long looking at one animal, that they miss others in the vicinity. This sometimes happens with Mysticetes because observers try to identify each animal to species. Again, a good field protocol can minimise the chances of this resulting in missing animals on the line. e.g. a second observer could be dedicated to identifying animals, perhaps using digital photography, once the first observer has detected them. Double-platform techniques can also be used to used to assess the proportion of animals missed on the track line but it's probably better not to miss them in the first place, if possible.
>
> Regards,
>
> Ewan
>

I thought I was done with my analysis and had a last minute panic moment. I would like advice regarding if I have completed my distance analysis appropriately or if I will need to go back and revise my output.

I have dolphin detections for two species of dolphins from a line transect ship survey completed during March-May of 2012, 2013 and 2014. The survey area is an MPA which was stratified into 3 regions: north, central and south due to cost effectiveness for only being able to survey the northern and southern strata with low effort per year. The survey design is a systematic parallel line survey; however, all lines were not repeated each year and some lines were only partially completed. I calculated segment length (i.e. the effort column) based on when there were changes in effort for search effort, changes in sea state, etc. Thus, multiple segments generally comprise a single transect line and I have treated these as individual units. Further, since segment length was calculated based on effort, the same transect lines that were completed in different years are not identical due to the segments which comprise them. For example, in 2012 Line X was only completed halfway. In 2014, the same Line X was completed in full but a portion of the line (i.e. segment X.2) was excluded due to bad weather. Due to all of this variability, I pooled all segments with appropriate search effort that occurred on dedicated transit legs from 2012-2014 and then stratified by region to estimate D and N.

Originally I thought this was the appropriate way to analyze the data because I have very low sample sizes.
Total detections on dedicated legs by region for dusky and Heaviside's dolphins, respectively:
North Region  =     7           8
Central Region = 60         17
South Region  =    1           8
Total =                  68         33

The survey region is located in the center of both of these species' distribution ranges. The amount of survey effort varied across years and regions. At the moment, my estimated CV's for overall abundance for both species are decent at around 20-38%. They are obviously higher for the northern and southern regions but due to the low effort in these regions, the weighted effort from the central region balances it out. If I was to have to further separate these data by 3 individual years, the low sample size issue would become an even bigger problem.

Here is the same output with stratification by region and year: NB* again, ignore row 'X': -- The values by year do appear to be quite different for this species

Any advice will be greatly appreciated!! About to submit this PhD chapter and nerves are setting in just a bit!

I would not present the year-specific estimates if you have used a common detection function. Susana

Welcome to the email group.  Hopefully this will help you get your data organised, so you can enjoy your estimates of avian density.  As an aside, going forward you might reconsider the duration of your point counts as point counts are sensitive to animal movement.  This is discussed in the following paper.

Buckland, S. T. 2006. Point-Transect Surveys for Songbirds: Robust Methodologies. The Auk 123 (2): 345–57. https://doi.org/10.1642/0004-8038(2006)123[345:PSFSRM]2.0.CO;2 <https://doi.org/10.1642/0004-8038(2006)123%5B345:PSFSRM%5D2.0.CO;2>.

Organising your data properly involves transmitting information about your survey design to program Distance.  You note you have a single stratum in your study area; but your study was conducted over three seasons.  Do you want a separate density estimate for each season?  If so, you could treat your seasons as strata--you may have already done that further down in your data (off the screen shot).  If you do not wish season-specific estimates, then no need to create strata for them.

Regarding the point transect layer of your data, I'm confused by the field "point".  If that is the name of the point, then I would have expected the data to have been sorted such that all CS1 detections appear together.  You should have used the field "Label" for the purpose of providing point names.  I'm also confused by the second and third rows of your data.  Both are labelled CS2, but have 3 and 2 for effort; the same point should not have two different levels of effort.

Next point of concern is "number of birds" in observation layer.  I presume this is flock size.  If so, that should not be a text field, but rather a field of type integer.  The software cannot treat those values as numbers if they are imported as text.

The "cloud cover" field has missing data (observations 4 and 5); Distance might not like covariates that are sometimes missing.

Regarding use of the data filter; I'll demonstrate with a project entitled "Songbird.dst":  this is in the "Sample Projects" directory that was installed on your computer when you installed Distance.  That project describes a survey that might be quite similar to your study; I suggest you study that project closely. Say you wish to estimate density for species SOSP (song sparrow):

I suspect you may not be able to estimate density for all 70 of your species, particularly the rare ones; but you can better judge this when you get further into your analysis.

Resources for more help: I've already mentioned the Songbird sample project that ships with Distance.  In addition, there are additional point transect datasets in Sample projects: "House Wren" and "Amakihi".  Beyond this, we have an online distance sampling workshop.  It contains a chapter on point transects (Chapter 3), with video lectures by Prof Buckland as well as an exercise based around the data he collected in association with the Buckland (2006) paper previously mentioned.

The online workshop can be accessed at
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/

Valentina

I'm not a spatial modelling expert, so I don't have the answers to the mystery.  I can't guess what the function gam() does with the argument `ddf.obj`; dsm() using that argument for the detectability adjustment--I wouldn't think gam() knows anything about that.

The only other light I can shine on this is that the source code for the dsm() function where the `weights` argument is defined:

    if (!(response %in% c("D", "density", "Dhat", "density.est",
        "presence"))) {
        formula <- as.formula(paste(c(as.character(formula)[c(2,
            1, 3)], "+ offset(off.set)"), collapse = ""))
    }
    else {
        if (is.null(weights)) {
            weights <- dat$segment.area
        }
        else if (length(weights) == 1) {
            weights <- rep(weights, nrow(dat))
        }
    }

Hi Valentina,

I think Eric's point about gam() not knowing what to do with distance information seems very valid. The point of distance analysis is that it deals with detectability issues. If a normal gam() could kick out the same co-efficients for a particular analysis it would call into question why you were using distance in the first place.

If you want to get closer to figuring out exactly what is causing the difference between the two approaches, you could replace the areas (being used as weights by the gam) with an invariant vector (e.g. "1") in order to rule it out of the equation, as it were. If you still have differences, you could begin to hone in on what they were. My guess is that it will be, as Eric has indicated, in the way that "ddf.obj" is used (or not) by these functions.

Cheers,

Mark

Yes, so as you can see from my gam formula, I don't insert the detection function at all as an argument as in a gam formula that doensn't make sense. What I did is to extract from the dsm output the abundance per segment (that is calculated thorough using the detection function and the number of observation in the segment and use it in a gam) and use it in a gam, so the detection function isn't a problem in itself.
DSM is supposedly running a gam on the abundance per segment vs the covariates and using segment area to weigh them. But I guess what eric said makes sense as in within the dsm function it's clearly written that the observation are weighted per area.

Hi folks,

I don't see anything wrong in the formulae you have here but I think
there might be some confusion over "weights" vs. "offsets" in the model.
They are the same in some cases but not others.

The DSM uses the offset take into account the area of the segment in the
estimated abundance case. The response is then the Horvitz-Thompson
estimate of the abundance in that segment (so detection-level
information is encapsulated in the response, see Miller et al (2013)).

You should get the same results running gam and dsm provided you have
the same data (as you are doing below extracting the data from the dsm
object), same offset and formula.

Note that the model object returned by dsm() **is** a gam object. It has
an extra class "dsm", so:

 > class(Model)
[1] "dsm" "gam" "glm" "lm"

which means you can use any functions from mgcv on that object.

The returned object also will have an extra element $ddf which has the
detection function information. So, most of the time this refitting is
not necessary.

cheers,
--dave

Hi Valentina, hi listfolks,

Inline responses below...

On 13/12/2018 13:46, Valentina Zini wrote:
> Yes, the offset terms makes sense for the Horvitz-Thompson estimation,
> what I would want is dsm to give more importance to those segments with
> greater length (and thus a bigger area surveyed provided they have the
> same ddf).

This is exactly what the offset does.

> I thought the weights argument was taking care of that.

The offset is effectively a model term with fixed coefficient 1. That
takes the density scale that the GAM normally works on to a scale of
number of animals, thus ensuring that the amount of effort is taken into
account.

Weights are used to change the "importance" of observations when fitting
the model (see e.g., the description of the weights argument in ?gam).
They don't change what the response means though, as offsets do. The
exact interpretation can be different in different software.

> Other than the non necessary refitting I would want to understand what
> is going on in the function.

The dsm source code is all on github to take a look at in more detail.
Briefly, all dsm really does is format the data into one data.frame,
including the information about detectability. It then runs gam() on
that resulting data.

> So what is happening in the gam is that because I included the offset
> term in the gam formula I am pretty much weighting each observation as
> offset and weights behave similarly in a gam? (Please forgive my ignorance)

Both offsets and weights can be used in both gam() and dsm() (as really
dsm() is just calling gam()). The offset will take into account varying
effort and ensure the response is on the scale of "number of animals".

See e.g., this post:
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/246318/difference-between-offset-and-weights
and links therein for more information on the difference between the
offsets and weights.

cheers,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Hello Distance list,

I come back to you for a new concern about point transect and left truncation.

5 point-transects have been performed to study ibex population (sampled since 2000, 2 or 3 times a year). Observers are not located physically within the observed population but at distances that vary according to the point-transect. For example, for the observation point n°1, observer is located on the other side of the valley, which allows the observer to see all the other side of the mountain where the population is (the observation points are easily accessible, that's why we chose this design. Going into the population to count them would require a lot of time, people and energy). Distances are calculated on a map from the observer to the clusters of individuals. This observer n°1 is located at  680 m from the first cluster of individuals. The distances between the observers and the closest cluster varies between point transect (e.g. observer n°2 is located at 370m from the closest cluster) and distances are never small or equal to 0.
An important point is that observers are generally separated from the other side of the mountain by the valley and a river where no individuals can be observed (because they never go there, low altitude).
This implies that we have to take into account a left-truncation in our data analysis. Right ?

1- Left-truncation distances varie between point transect, how do we deal with this in the "ds" function with R (as the left-truncation only requires a single number) ?
2- Should we analyse each point transect individually even if it decreases the power of the analysis ?
3- Should we use left-truncation (assuming g(x) is different to 1 at the truncation point) or substract the truncation distances (different according to point transect) from all the data (assuming that g(x)=1 at the truncation distance) ? The latter case would imply that the location of the observer is not important in the observation, which is not true.

It is not very easy to explain, I hope you will understand my problem !

Thanks a lot for your help

Cheers
Marjorie

Hi Marjorie,

I remember your situation from a previous post. It struck me at the time that it might be possible to justify a distance-based approach if you could reasonably assume that ibex in the nearest portion of the counting area were detected with close to 100% efficiency. I can imagine situations in which this was the case and it might be possible to operate an analysis where your 'zero' started at the nearest distance that you could detect animals (assuming detection probability of 1). However, in the circumstances you described there are a number of complications:

1. I have no idea whether and how strongly you could argue that detection probability of ibex in the nearest distance band was 100%. If it is likely to be less than this, it would likely be a difficult parameter to get a decent estimate of. Something like an intensive study involving remote-tracking of GPS or VHF tagged animals, where you could calibrate survey observations with known positions of marked animals, might provide you with the information you needed... but would probably require a prohibitive level of resourcing!

2. In the situation you are describing, I think it is likely that detectability would vary not only with distance from observer, but also direction. Animals 2km away on a steep slope and straight in front of you would probably be more visible than animals 2km away and off to the side, on less steeply sloping ground. With enough data, you might be able to get around this by assigning animals to different detection zones, and working out detectability for each zone relative to the nearest and most visible zone (where you would assume 100%).

3. Much more problematic, for distance sampling, is the fact that the actual distribution of animals over the area in which you are detecting them is unlikely to be random with respect to distance. This would mean that comparing the densities detected at different distances (or in different detection zones) can't straightforwardly be interpreted in terms of detectability, as you can't distinguish them from real differences in density.

On the plus side, counts from set points, using standardised effort, experience, equipment etc. should be good indices of abundance, even if it's hard or impossible to interpret them in absolute abundance terms.

As you can see, I haven't really offered a solution to you. I am intrigued to see what the more expert distance analysts on the list can recommend!

Cheers,

Mark

Marjorie

I concur with Mark's points 1-3.

I'm trying to think of ways this survey design might work, but I'm afraid I identify more challenges this design possesses.  Recognise that even if the design was perfect, drawing inference from 5 transects will limit you ability to accurately estimate encounter rate variability.  The fewer transects, the more suspect is the inference extended from those 5 transects to a broader study area.  You also note "observation points are easily accessible" hence they are not representative of the study area.  Along with the non-representativeness Mark's issue 3 about distribution of animals with respect to distance from the point also arises in your design.

Now to the matter that the observers are not situated at the centre of the point transect, rather are located at "distance that are never small."  I wonder how much ibex detectability would actually vary as a function of distance from the transect centre under your design.  Central tenet of distance sampling is the existence of information in detection distance to help estimate detection probability through fitting a detection function.  I am sceptical that information content of detection distance in this situation would be of much use in producing a defensible estimate of detection probability.

Independent of the mechanics of performing left-truncation upon the data, I would be reluctant to perform a distance sampling analysis upon these data as I would be dubious of the result.
